name: Ectrodactyly-Ectodermal Dysplasia-Clefting Syndrome
aliases: Split hand-split foot with ectodermal dysplasia and clefting

clinicalPearls: EEC syndrome is defined by the triad of ectrodactyly (split hand or split foot), ectodermal dysplasia and orofacial clefting, though expression is highly variable.
Most cases arise from heterozygous missense variants in TP63, typically clustering in the DNA-binding domain, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with variable penetrance.
Ectodermal features include sparse light-coloured hair, hypodontia with conical teeth, nail dystrophy and hypoplastic sweat and other exocrine glands.
Lacrimal duct anomalies are characteristic, producing chronic tearing, recurrent dacryocystitis and predisposition to keratitis.
Genitourinary anomalies including hydronephrosis, vesicoureteric reflux and duplex systems are common and warrant renal tract screening.
TP63 variants underlie an allelic spectrum that also includes AEC (Hay-Wells), limb-mammary, ADULT and split hand-foot malformation syndromes.
Progressive corneal changes and limbal stem cell deficiency can threaten sight and require ophthalmological surveillance.
Conductive hearing loss and recurrent respiratory or middle-ear infection relate to glandular hypoplasia and clefting.
reference.pathophysiology: EEC syndrome results from heterozygous, usually missense, variants in TP63, a transcription factor of the p53 family that is a master regulator of epithelial development. The dominant isoform in stratified epithelia governs the proliferation and commitment of epidermal and limb apical ectodermal ridge progenitors and the morphogenesis of skin appendages, teeth, exocrine glands and the anterior ocular surface. Variants in the DNA-binding domain typically act through a dominant-negative or altered-function mechanism, perturbing the transcriptional programmes that maintain epithelial stem cell populations. Failure of apical ectodermal ridge signalling during limb outgrowth produces the central ray deficiency of ectrodactyly, while disrupted epithelial-mesenchymal interaction during facial fusion yields cleft lip and palate. The same impaired epithelial differentiation underlies the ectodermal dysplasia phenotype, including hair, nail, dental and glandular hypoplasia, and the lacrimal and corneal epithelial defects that endanger vision. The particular variant location within TP63 largely determines which overlapping allelic phenotype predominates.
additionalDifferentials: Limb-mammary syndrome and ADULT syndrome (allelic TP63 disorders)
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of TP63 with correlation to the clinical subtype
Radiography of hands and feet to define the limb malformation
Renal tract ultrasound and, where indicated, further urological imaging
Ophthalmological assessment including lacrimal drainage and corneal surface evaluation
Dental and orthodontic assessment with panoramic radiography
Audiological testing for conductive and mixed hearing loss
redFlags: Progressive corneal opacification or ulceration threatening vision
Recurrent urinary tract infection or hydronephrosis indicating significant renal tract anomaly
Feeding difficulty and failure to thrive in the infant with orofacial clefting
reference.prognosis: Lifespan is generally normal, and multidisciplinary care of clefting, limb, dental, renal and ocular manifestations gives good functional outcomes, though progressive corneal disease is an important cause of long-term visual morbidity.
pitfalls: Assuming the full triad must be present, when incomplete or asymmetric expression is common
Overlooking asymptomatic renal tract anomalies because urinary screening was not performed
Missing evolving limbal stem cell deficiency by neglecting ophthalmological follow-up
Failing to distinguish EEC from allelic TP63 disorders that carry different associated risks
Underestimating recurrence risk given autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity
references: Dermatology and ectodermal dysplasia reference texts
